claim: BonVision is an open-source software package for the display of virtual or augmented reality, as well as standard visual stimuli.
source: We developed BonVision as an easy-to-use open-source software for the display of virtual or augmented reality, as well as standard visual stimuli.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of what was developed.

claim: BonVision has been tested on humans and mice.
source: BonVision has been tested on humans and mice, and is capable of supporting new experimental designs in other animal models of vision.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that testing was performed on these species.

claim: BonVision is based on the open-source Bonsai graphical programming language.
source: As the architecture is based on the open-source Bonsai graphical programming language, BonVision benefits from native integration with experimental hardware.
evidence: The abstract directly states the architectural foundation of BonVision.

claim: BonVision enables easy implementation of closed-loop experiments, including real-time interaction with deep neural networks.
source: BonVision therefore enables easy implementation of closed-loop experiments, including real-time interaction with deep neural networks, and communication with behavioural and physiological measurement and manipulation devices.
evidence: This capability is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: Gaming-driven advances in computation and graphical rendering have driven the development of immersive closed-loop visual environments.
source: Gaming-driven advances in computation and graphical rendering have driven the development of immersive closed-loop visual environments, but these new platforms are not readily amenable to traditional research paradigms.
evidence: This is stated as background context in the introduction.

claim: Gaming-driven platforms do not specify an image in egocentric units (of visual angle).
source: For example, they do not specify an image in egocentric units (of visual angle), sacrifice precise control of a visual display, and lack transparent interaction with external hardware.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of gaming platforms in the introduction.

claim: Most vision research has been performed in non-immersive environments with standard two-dimensional visual stimuli.
source: Most vision research has been performed in non-immersive environments with standard two-dimensional visual stimuli, such as gratings or dot stimuli, using established platforms including PsychToolbox (Brainard, 1997) or PsychoPy (Peirce, 2007; Peirce, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as background context with citations to support the claim.

claim: STYTRA provides 2D visual stimuli for larval zebrafish in python.
source: STYTRA (Štih et al., 2019) provides 2D visual stimuli for larval zebrafish in python
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the STYTRA paper.

claim: ratCAVE is a specialised augmented reality system for rodents in python.
source: ratCAVE (Del Grosso and Sirota, 2019) is a specialised augmented reality system for rodents in python
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the ratCAVE paper.

claim: FreemoVR provides virtual reality in Ubuntu/Linux.
source: FreemoVR (Stowers et al., 2017) provides virtual reality in Ubuntu/Linux
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the FreemoVR paper.

claim: ViRMEn provides virtual reality in Matlab.
source: ViRMEn (Aronov and Tank, 2014) provides virtual reality in Matlab
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the ViRMEn paper.

claim: New platforms for closed-loop visual stimulus generation lack the generalised frameworks needed to specify or present standard visual stimuli.
source: However, these new platforms lack the generalised frameworks needed to specify or present standard visual stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing platforms in the introduction.

claim: BonVision exploits Bonsai's ability to run OpenGL commands on the graphics card through the Bonsai.Shaders package.
source: BonVision exploits Bonsai's ability to run OpenGL commands on the graphics card through the Bonsai.Shaders package.
evidence: This is stated as a technical implementation detail in the introduction.

claim: BonVision provides pre-built GPU shaders and resources for stimuli used in vision research.
source: BonVision further extends Bonsai by providing pre-built GPU shaders and resources for stimuli used in vision research, including movies, along with an accessible, modular interface for composing stimuli and designing experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of BonVision in the introduction.

claim: The definition of stimuli in BonVision is independent of the display hardware.
source: The definition of stimuli in BonVision is independent of the display hardware, allowing for easy replication of workflows across different experimental configurations.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of BonVision in the introduction.

claim: BonVision can automatically detect and define the relationship between the observer and the display from a photograph of the experimental apparatus.
source: Additional unique features include the ability to automatically detect and define the relationship between the observer and the display from a photograph of the experimental apparatus, and to use the outputs of real-time inference methods to determine the position and pose of an observer online, thereby generating augmented reality environments.
evidence: This is stated as a unique feature in the introduction.

claim: BonVision maps the 2D retino-centric coordinate frame to the surface of a 3D sphere using the Mercator projection.
source: We achieved this by mapping the 2D retino-centric coordinate frame (i.e. degrees of the visual field) to the surface of a 3D sphere using the Mercator projection (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: BonVision uses 'cube mapping' to specify the 360° projection of 3D environments onto arbitrary viewpoints around an experimental observer.
source: We then used 'cube mapping' to specify the 360° projection of 3D environments onto arbitrary viewpoints around an experimental observer (human or animal; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: BonVision makes it easy to replicate visual environments and experimental designs on various display devices, including multiple monitors, curved projection surfaces, and head-mounted displays.
source: Consequently, BonVision makes it easy to replicate visual environments and experimental designs on various display devices, including multiple monitors, curved projection surfaces, and head-mounted displays (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1C-E.

claim: BonVision features a fast semi-automated display calibration using a photograph of the experimental setup with fiducial markers.
source: To facilitate easy and rapid porting between different experimental apparatus, BonVision features a fast semi-automated display calibration. A photograph of the experimental setup with fiducial markers (Garrido-Jurado et al., 2014) measures the 3D position and orientation of each display relative to the observer (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: BonVision's inbuilt image processing algorithms estimate the position and orientation of each marker to fully specify the display environment.
source: BonVision's inbuilt image processing algorithms then estimate the position and orientation of each marker to fully specify the display environment.
evidence: This is stated as a technical capability in the Results section.

claim: BonVision has a library of standard pre-defined 3D structures including planes, spheres, and cubes.
source: BonVision has a library of standard pre-defined 3D structures (including planes, spheres, and cubes), and environments can be defined by specifying the position and scale of the structures, and the textures rendered on them (e.g. Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: BonVision has the ability to import standard format 3D design files created elsewhere.
source: BonVision also has the ability to import standard format 3D design files created elsewhere in order to generate more complex environments (file formats listed in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a capability in the Results section.

claim: BonVision can define the relationship between the display and the observer in real-time.
source: BonVision can define the relationship between the display and the observer in real-time.
evidence: This is stated as a capability in the Results section.

claim: BonVision enables closed-loop, position-dependent updating of displays when a mouse navigates through an arena surrounded by displays.
source: For example, when a mouse navigates through an arena surrounded by displays, BonVision enables closed-loop, position-dependent updating of those displays.
evidence: This is stated as an example application in the Results section.

claim: Bonsai has turn-key capacity for real-time live pose estimation techniques using deep neural networks.
source: Bonsai can track markers to determine the position of the observer, but it also has turn-key capacity for real-time live pose estimation techniques – using deep neural networks (Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2019; Kane et al., 2020) – to keep track of the observer's movements.
evidence: This is stated with citations to relevant papers in the Results section.

claim: BonVision is capable of rendering visual environments near the limits of the hardware.
source: BonVision is capable of rendering visual environments near the limits of the hardware (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Bonsai is based on a just-in-time compiler architecture such that there is little computational overhead.
source: This is possible because Bonsai is based on a just-in-time compiler architecture such that there is little computational overhead.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for performance in the Results section.

claim: BonVision's closed-loop latency averaged 2.11 ± 0.78 frames (35.26 ± 13.07 ms) when a monitor was refreshed at 60 Hz.
source: We found delays averaged 2.11 ± 0.78 frames (35.26 ± 13.07 ms).
evidence: This is a measured result reported in the Results section.

claim: BonVision's latency was slightly shorter than that achieved by PsychToolbox on the same laptop.
source: This latency was slightly shorter than that achieved by PsychToolbox (Brainard, 1997) on the same laptop (2.44 ± 0.59 frames, 40.73 ± 9.8 ms; Welch's t-test, p<10−80, n = 1000).
evidence: This is a comparative result with statistical testing reported in the Results section.

claim: Higher frame rate displays yielded lower latency in BonVision.
source: The overall latency of BonVision was mainly constrained by the refresh rate of the display device, such that higher frame rate displays yielded lower latency (60 Hz: 35.26 ± 13.07 ms; 90 Hz: 28.45 ± 7.22 ms; 144 Hz: 18.49 ± 10.1 ms; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a measured result reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BonVision was able to render up to 576 independent elements at 60 Hz without missing frames.
source: BonVision was able to render up to 576 independent elements and up to eight overlapping textures at 60 Hz without missing ('dropping') frames, broadly matching PsychoPy (Peirce, 2007; Peirce, 2008) and Psychtoolbox (Brainard, 1997).
evidence: This is a benchmarking result reported in the Results section.

claim: BonVision was able to render up to eight overlapping textures at 60 Hz without missing frames.
source: BonVision was able to render up to 576 independent elements and up to eight overlapping textures at 60 Hz without missing ('dropping') frames, broadly matching PsychoPy (Peirce, 2007; Peirce, 2008) and Psychtoolbox (Brainard, 1997).
evidence: This is a benchmarking result reported in the Results section.

claim: BonVision supports video playback, either by preloading the video or by streaming it from the disk.
source: BonVision also supports video playback, either by preloading the video or by streaming it from the disk.
evidence: This is stated as a capability in the Results section.

claim: BonVision's streaming mode is capable of displaying both standard definition (SD: 480 p) and full HD (HD: 1080 p) at 60 Hz on a standard computer.
source: The streaming mode, which utilises real-time file I/O and decompression, is capable of displaying both standard definition (SD: 480 p) and full HD (HD: 1080 p) at 60 Hz on a standard computer (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a performance result reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: BonVision is capable of running on Linux.
source: We benchmarked BonVision on a standard Windows OS laptop, but BonVision is now also capable of running on Linux.
evidence: This is stated as a capability in the Results section.

claim: BonVision's rendering speed and timing accuracy are sufficient to support neurophysiological experiments.
source: To confirm that the rendering speed and timing accuracy of BonVision are sufficient to support neurophysiological experiments, which need high timing precision, we mapped the receptive fields of neurons early in the visual pathway (Yeh et al., 2009), in the mouse primary visual cortex and superior colliculus.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from experimental validation in the Results section.

claim: Receptive fields were recovered from electrophysiological measurements in the superior colliculus and primary visual cortex of awake mice using BonVision.
source: In our experiments using BonVision, we were able to recover receptive fields from electrophysiological measurements - both in the superior colliculus and primary visual cortex of awake mice (Figure 5B and C) – demonstrating that BonVision meets the timing requirements for visual neurophysiology.
evidence: This is an experimental result reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: BonVision's independent logging of stimulus presentation timing was sufficient to capture the receptive field.
source: BonVision's independent logging of stimulus presentation timing was also sufficient to capture the receptive field (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a validation result in the Results section with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: All human observers were able to identify which cube was larger in the virtual reality depth perception task using BonVision.
source: Distinguishing objects of the same retinal size required observers to use depth-dependent cues (Rolland et al., 1995), and we found that all observers were able to identify which cube was larger (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an experimental result reported in the Results section with a citation and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mouse locomotion speed increased with repeated exposure to the virtual platform in BonVision.
source: Not only did mouse locomotion speed increase with repeated exposure, but the animals modulated their speed depending on their location in the platform (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is an experimental result reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Mice modulated their speed depending on their location in the virtual platform.
source: Not only did mouse locomotion speed increase with repeated exposure, but the animals modulated their speed depending on their location in the platform (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is an experimental result reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Visual stimuli presented in BonVision primarily elicited a freezing response in freely moving mice.
source: Visual stimuli presented in BonVision primarily elicited a freezing response, which similar experiments have previously described (De Franceschi et al., 2016; Figure 5I).
evidence: This is an experimental result reported in the Results section with a citation and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: BonVision provides sufficient rendering performance to support human and animal visual behaviour.
source: Together these results show that BonVision provides sufficient rendering performance to support human and animal visual behaviour.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results in the Results section.

claim: BonVision is a single software package to support experimental designs that require visual display, including virtual and augmented reality environments.
source: BonVision is a single software package to support experimental designs that require visual display, including virtual and augmented reality environments.
evidence: This is stated as a summary in the Discussion section.

claim: BonVision is easy and fast to implement, cross-platform and open source.
source: BonVision is easy and fast to implement, cross-platform and open source, providing versatility and reproducibility.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of features in the Discussion section.

claim: BonVision's architecture separates specification of the display and the visual environment.
source: This is possible because BonVision's architecture separates specification of the display and the visual environment.
evidence: This is stated as an architectural feature in the Discussion section.

claim: BonVision includes a library of workflows and operators to standardise and ease the construction of new stimuli and virtual environments.
source: Second, BonVision includes a library of workflows and operators to standardise and ease the construction of new stimuli and virtual environments.
evidence: This is stated as a feature in the Discussion section.

claim: The modular structure of BonVision enables the development and exchange of custom nodes for generating new visual stimuli or functionality.
source: In addition, the modular structure of BonVision enables the development and exchange of custom nodes for generating new visual stimuli or functionality without the need to construct the complete experimental paradigm.
evidence: This is stated as a feature in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai has a large user base and an active developer community.
source: Third, BonVision is based on Bonsai (Lopes et al., 2015), which has a large user base and an active developer community, and is now a standard tool for open-source neuroscience research.
evidence: This is stated with a citation in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai is now a standard tool for open-source neuroscience research.
source: Third, BonVision is based on Bonsai (Lopes et al., 2015), which has a large user base and an active developer community, and is now a standard tool for open-source neuroscience research.
evidence: This is stated with a citation in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai is widely used in applications including real-time video processing.
source: BonVision naturally integrates Bonsai's established packages in the multiple domains important for modern neuroscience, which are widely used in applications including real-time video processing (Zacarias et al., 2018; Buccino et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated with citations in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai is widely used in optogenetics applications.
source: optogenetics (Zacarias et al., 2018; Buccino et al., 2018; Moreira et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with citations in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai is widely used in fibre photometry applications.
source: fibre photometry (Soares et al., 2016; Hrvatin et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated with citations in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai is widely used in electrophysiology applications.
source: electrophysiology (including specific packages for Open Ephys Siegle et al., 2017; Neto et al., 2016 and high-density silicon probes Jun et al., 2017; Dimitriadis, 2018)
evidence: This is stated with citations in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai is widely used in calcium imaging applications.
source: calcium imaging (e.g. UCLA miniscope Aharoni et al., 2019; Cai et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with citations in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai workflows can be called via the command line.
source: Moreover, since Bonsai workflows can be called via the command line, BonVision can also be integrated into pre-existing, specialised frameworks in established laboratories.
evidence: This is stated as a capability in the Discussion section.

claim: BonVision can generate complex 3D environments and retinotopically defined 2D visual stimuli within the same framework.
source: In summary, BonVision can generate complex 3D environments and retinotopically defined 2D visual stimuli within the same framework.
evidence: This is stated as a summary in the Discussion section.

claim: Existing platforms used for vision research, including PsychToolbox, PsychoPy, STYTRA, or RigBox, focus on well-defined 2D stimuli.
source: Existing platforms used for vision research, including PsychToolbox (Brainard, 1997), PsychoPy (Peirce, 2007; Peirce, 2008), STYTRA (Štih et al., 2019), or RigBox (Bhagat et al., 2020), focus on well-defined 2D stimuli.
evidence: This is stated with citations in the Discussion section.

claim: Gaming-driven software, including FreemoVR, ratCAVE, and ViRMEn, are oriented towards generating virtual reality environments.
source: Similarly, gaming-driven software, including FreemoVR (Stowers et al., 2017), ratCAVE (Del Grosso and Sirota, 2019), and ViRMEn (Aronov and Tank, 2014), are oriented towards generating virtual reality environments.
evidence: This is stated with citations in the Discussion section.

claim: BonVision brings the unique capacity to automatically calibrate the display environment.
source: BonVision combines the advantages of both these approaches in a single framework (Appendix 1), while bringing the unique capacity to automatically calibrate the display environment, and use deep neural networks to provide real-time control of virtual environments.
evidence: This is stated as a unique feature in the Discussion section.

claim: BonVision can use deep neural networks to provide real-time control of virtual environments.
source: BonVision combines the advantages of both these approaches in a single framework (Appendix 1), while bringing the unique capacity to automatically calibrate the display environment, and use deep neural networks to provide real-time control of virtual environments.
evidence: This is stated as a unique feature in the Discussion section.

claim: Experiments in BonVision can be rapidly prototyped and easily replicated across different display configurations.
source: Experiments in BonVision can be rapidly prototyped and easily replicated across different display configurations.
evidence: This is stated as a feature in the Discussion section.

claim: BonVision is free, open-source, and portable.
source: Being free, open-source, and portable, BonVision is a state-of-the-art tool for visual display that is accessible to the wider community.
evidence: This is stated as a summary in the Discussion section.

claim: All animal experiments were performed in accordance with the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 (United Kingdom).
source: All experiments were performed in accordance with the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 (United Kingdom) and Home Office (United Kingdom) approved project and personal licenses.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The experiments were approved by the University College London Animal Welfare Ethical Review Board under Project License 70/8637.
source: The experiments were approved by the University College London Animal Welfare Ethical Review Board under Project License 70/8637.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The mice used were C57BL6 wild-type.
source: The mice (C57BL6 wild-type) were group-housed with a maximum of five to a cage, under a 12 hr light/dark cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All behavioural and electrophysiological recordings were carried out during the dark phase of the cycle.
source: All behavioural and electrophysiological recordings were carried out during the dark phase of the cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Freezing was defined as a drop in the animal speed below 2 cm/s that lasted more than 0.1 s.
source: Freezing was defined as a drop in the animal speed below 2 cm/s that lasted more than 0.1 s; flight responses as an increase in the animal running speed above 40 cm/s (De Franceschi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological definition in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Flight responses were defined as an increase in the animal running speed above 40 cm/s.
source: Freezing was defined as a drop in the animal speed below 2 cm/s that lasted more than 0.1 s; flight responses as an increase in the animal running speed above 40 cm/s (De Franceschi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological definition in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Multi-electrode array probes with two shanks and 32 channels were used to record neural activity.
source: To record neural activity, we used multi-electrode array probes with two shanks and 32 channels (ASSY-37 E-1, Cambridge Neurotech Ltd., Cambridge, UK).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Electrophysiology data was acquired with an Open Ephys acquisition board connected to a different computer from that used to generate the visual stimulus.
source: Electrophysiology data was acquired with an Open Ephys acquisition board connected to a different computer from that used to generate the visual stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The electrophysiological data from each session was processed using Kilosort 1 or Kilosort 2.
source: The electrophysiological data from each session was processed using Kilosort 1 or Kilosort 2 (Pachitariu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail with a citation in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A ResNet-50 network was trained using DeepLabCut for mouse tracking.
source: A ResNet-50 network was trained using DeepLabCut (Mathis et al., 2018; Kane et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail with citations in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The position of the animal was updated from the video file at a rate of 40 frames/s on a gaming laptop.
source: The position of the animal was updated from the video file at a rate of 40 frames/s on a gaming laptop: ASUS ROG Zephyrus GX501GI, with an Intel Core i7-8750H (six cores, 2.20 GHz), 16 GB RAM, equipped with a NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080, using a 512 × 512 video.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: BonVision is compatible with different headsets including Oculus Rift and HTC Vive.
source: BonVision is compatible with different headsets (e.g. Oculus Rift, HTC Vive).
evidence: This is stated as a compatibility feature in the Materials and methods section.

claim: BonVision receives the projection matrix and the view matrix for each eye from the head set.
source: BonVision receives the projection matrix (perspective projection of world display) and the view matrix (position of eye in the world) for each eye from the head set.
evidence: This is stated as a technical detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: BonVision uses matrices from the headset to generate two textures, one for the left eye and one for the right eye.
source: BonVision uses these matrices to generate two textures, one for the left eye and one for the right eye.
evidence: This is stated as a technical detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: BonVision is available under the MIT license.
source: BonVision is an open-source software package available to use under the MIT license.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: BonVision can be downloaded through the Bonsai package manager.
source: It can be downloaded through the Bonsai (bonsai-rx.org) package manager, and the source code is available at: github.com/bonvision/BonVision.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: BonVision source code is available at github.com/bonvision/BonVision.
source: It can be downloaded through the Bonsai (bonsai-rx.org) package manager, and the source code is available at: github.com/bonvision/BonVision.

claim: BonVision supports the following image formats: PNG, JPG, BMP, TIFF, and GIF.
source: We confirmed the ability to use the following image formats: PNG, JPG, BMP, TIFF, and GIF.
evidence: This is stated as a tested capability in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Movie display in BonVision relies on the FFmpeg library.
source: Movie display relies on the FFmpeg library (https://ffmpeg.org/), an industry standard
evidence: This is stated as a technical detail in the Materials and methods section.

source: we confirmed ability to use the following containers: AVI, MP4, OGG, OGV, and WMV
evidence: This is stated as a tested capability in the Materials and methods section.

claim: BonVision supports the following codecs: H264, MPEG4, MPEG2, DIVX.
source: in conjunction with standard codecs: H264, MPEG4, MPEG2, DIVX
evidence: This is stated as a tested capability in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Importing 3D models and complex scenes in BonVision relies on the Open Asset Importer Library (Assimp).
source: Importing 3D models and complex scenes relies on the Open Asset Importer Library (Assimp | http://assimp.org/).
evidence: This is stated as a technical detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: BonVision can import and render 3D models and scenes from the following formats: OBJ, Blender.
source: We confirmed the ability to import and render 3D models and scenes from the following formats: OBJ, Blender.

claim: BonVision maps 2D stimuli onto a sphere to unify 2D and 3D visual presentation.
source: We achieved this by mapping the 2D retino-centric coordinate frame (i.e. degrees of the visual field) to the surface of a 3D sphere using the Mercator projection (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The resulting sphere could therefore be rendered onto displays in the same way as any other 3D environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the description of the technical approach to unifying 2D and 3D presentation.

claim: The number of frames between external event and stimulus presentation was similar across different frame rates in BonVision.
source: That is, the number of frames between the external event and stimulus presentation was similar across frame rate (60 Hz: 2.11 ± 0.78 frames; 90 Hz: 2.56 ± 0.65 frames; 144 Hz: 2.66 ± 1.45 frames; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a measured result reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: BonVision achieved slightly fewer overlapping textures than PsychoPy because BonVision does not currently have the option to trade-off the resolution of a texture and its mask for performance.
source: BonVision achieved slightly fewer overlapping textures than PsychoPy, as BonVision does not currently have the option to trade-off the resolution of a texture and its mask for performance.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for a performance difference in the Results section.

claim: At higher rates, performance for Full HD videos is impaired, but is improved by buffering, and fully restored by preloading the video onto memory.
source: At higher rates, performance is impaired for Full HD videos, but is improved by buffering, and fully restored by preloading the video onto memory (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a performance result reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The sparse noise stimulus is sensitive to the timing accuracy of the visual stimulus.
source: This stimulus, which is commonly used to measure receptive fields of visual neurons, is sensitive to the timing accuracy of the visual stimulus, meaning that errors in timing would prevent the identification of receptive fields.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the stimulus in the Results section.

claim: Errors in timing would prevent the identification of receptive fields using sparse noise stimuli.
source: This stimulus, which is commonly used to measure receptive fields of visual neurons, is sensitive to the timing accuracy of the visual stimulus, meaning that errors in timing would prevent the identification of receptive fields.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of timing errors in the Results section.

claim: Bonsai requires researchers to get accustomed to its graphical interface and event-based framework.
source: Bonsai requires researchers to get accustomed to its graphical interface and event-based framework.
evidence: This is stated as a learning requirement in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai reduces the time required to learn real-time programming after researchers get accustomed to it.
source: However, it subsequently reduces the time required to learn real-time programming, and the time to build new interfaces with external devices (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as a benefit in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai reduces the time to build new interfaces with external devices.
source: However, it subsequently reduces the time required to learn real-time programming, and the time to build new interfaces with external devices (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as a benefit in the Discussion section.

claim: BonVision can be integrated into pre-existing, specialised frameworks in established laboratories.
source: Moreover, since Bonsai workflows can be called via the command line, BonVision can also be integrated into pre-existing, specialised frameworks in established laboratories.

claim: BonVision is a state-of-the-art tool for visual display that is accessible to the wider community.
source: Being free, open-source, and portable, BonVision is a state-of-the-art tool for visual display that is accessible to the wider community.

claim: Benchmarking was performed on a Dell Latitude 7480 laptop with Intel Core i7-6600U Processor and Integrated HD Graphics 520 for 60 Hz tests.
source: For benchmarks at 60 Hz refresh rate, we used a standard laptop with the following configuration: Dell Latitude 7480, Intel Core i7-6600U Processor Base with Integrated HD Graphics 520 (Dual Core, 2.6 GHz), 16 GB RAM.

claim: For higher refresh rates, benchmarking used an ASUS ROG Zephyrus GX501GI gaming laptop with Intel Core i7-8750H and NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080.

claim: All benchmarking tests were run on Windows 10 Pro 64-bit.
source: All tests were run on Windows 10 Pro 64-bit.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: HARP devices from Champalimaud Research Scientific Hardware Platform were used to measure latency and dropped frames.
source: To measure the time from input detection to display update, as well as dropped frames detection, we used open-source HARP devices from Champalimaud Research Scientific Hardware Platform, using the Bonsai.HARP package.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The minimal latency for any update is typically two frames: one for VSync and one for OS delay.
source: Typically, the minimal latency for any update is two frames: one which is needed for the VSync, and one is the delay introduced by the OS.
evidence: This is stated as a technical explanation in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Display hardware can add further delays if they include additional buffering.
source: Display hardware can add further delays if they include additional buffering.
evidence: This is stated as a technical explanation in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Five male, 8-week-old, C57BL6 mice were used for the virtual reality behaviour experiment.
source: Five male, 8-week-old, C57BL6 mice were used for this experiment.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Mice were habituated to the virtual reality environment by progressively increasing the time spent head fixed from ~15 min to 2 hr.
source: One week after the surgery, mice were placed on a treadmill and habituated to the virtual reality (VR) environment by progressively increasing the number of time spent head fixed: from ~15 min to 2 hr.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Mice spontaneously ran on the treadmill, moving through the VR in absence of reward.
source: Mice spontaneously ran on the treadmill, moving through the VR in absence of reward.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The VR environment was a 100 cm long platform with a patterned texture.
source: The VR environment was a 100 cm long platform with a patterned texture that animals ran over for multiple trials.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Spike times were synchronized with behavioural data by aligning the signal of a photodiode that detected the visual stimuli transitions.
source: We synchronised spike times with behavioural data by aligning the signal of a photodiode that detected the visual stimuli transitions (PDA25K2, Thorlabs, Inc, USA).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Firing rate was sampled at 60 Hz and smoothed with a 300 ms Gaussian filter.
source: We sampled the firing rate at 60 Hz, and then smoothed it with a 300 ms Gaussian filter.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Receptive fields were calculated as the average firing rate or local field potential elicited by the appearance of a stimulus in each location.
source: We calculated receptive fields as the average firing rate or local field potential elicited by the appearance of a stimulus in each location (custom routines in MATLAB).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The position inference from the deep neural network and the BonVision visual stimulus rendering were run on the same machine.
source: The position inference from the deep neural network and the BonVision visual stimulus rendering were run on the same machine.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Performance can be improved using a lower pixel resolution for video capture, achieving up to 80 frames/s without a noticeable decrease in tracking accuracy.
source: The performance can be improved using a lower pixel resolution for video capture, and we were able to achieve up to 80 frames/s without a noticeable decrease in tracking accuracy using this strategy.
evidence: This is stated as a performance optimization result in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Further enhancements in tracking performance can be achieved using a MobileNetV2 network.
source: Further enhancements can be achieved using a MobileNetV2 network (Kane et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Four male participants were tested for the human psychophysics experiment.
source: Four male participants were tested for this experiment.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The human psychophysics experiments were run on a gaming laptop connected to a Vive Pro SteamVR head-mounted display (90 Hz refresh rate).
source: The experiments were run on a gaming laptop (described above) connected to a Vive Pro SteamVR head-mounted display (90 Hz refresh rate).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Standard onboard computations on the headset provide additional non-linear transformations that account for the relationship between the eye and the display.
source: Standard onboard computations on the headset provide additional non-linear transformations that account for the relationship between the eye and the display (such as lens distortion effects).
evidence: This is stated as a technical detail in the Materials and methods section.
